content.content:
1	A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is used to move glass panes, stone slabs, and similar flat panels on site by suction gripping. A suction cup is pressed against the face of the panel, air is removed from the space enclosed between the cup and the panel, and the resulting difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in that enclosed space clamps the cup to the panel so that the panel can be carried.
2	
3	A suction grip is only as good as its seal. Dust on the panel, a textured or porous surface, a nick in the sealing lip, a change in temperature, or simply the slow permeation and leakage that occurs over minutes of handling will all bleed air back into the enclosed space. As air returns, the clamping force falls. The failure is progressive and, from the point of view of the person holding the panel, silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes until the cup lets go, at which point a heavy panel is already falling.
4	
5	Vacuum lifting equipment has therefore long been fitted with vacuum monitoring. In one known lifter for transporting loads having an adhesion surface, a suction plate assembly carries projecting annular seals defining a vacuum chamber connected to a main vacuum source, a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that can be started by an emergency switch is additionally provided, and a pressure pickup associated with the vacuum chamber is coupled with a malfunction alarm such that the alarm is turned on when a preset limit pressure is exceeded during vacuum operation [REF:US-5310232-A]. That equipment is a suspended plate assembly with a main vacuum source and a separate emergency vacuum source; the alarm is described as a malfunction alarm tied to a preset limit pressure, and the reference does not describe the limit pressure in terms of the vacuum still needed to keep hold of the load.
6	
7	Control systems for vacuum lift equipment have also been described in which a programmable controller interprets feedback from vacuum level sensors and battery sensors and responsively provides warnings and limits or alters machine functions, including evaluating a change in measured vacuum level over time to determine a rate of vacuum level change that may be caused by a leak and outputting a warning indication when that rate exceeds a threshold rate [REF:US-10518985-B2]. Such a system is built around a controller with memory, stored records, and machine-function interlocks, and its leak warning is a response to how fast the vacuum is changing rather than to where the vacuum sits relative to the point at which the grip would fail.
8	
9	Powered suction devices in a hand-carried format are also known. An electric vacuum suction lifter has been described having a main body with a suction surface carrying first and second annular sealing units that bound a sealed space, a control unit, a vacuum pump controlled by the control unit to draw air from the sealed space, a pressure sensing unit that measures the pressure of the sealed space to generate instant pressure information, a battery unit that is charged by external power equipment and powers the control unit, pump, and pressure sensing unit, a start button, a pressure relief button, and at least one handle by which a member gripped by the device can be carried [REF:US-10625955-B2]. In that device the instant pressure information is compared with a high predetermined pressure and a low predetermined pressure: reaching the high predetermined pressure stops the pump, and falling below the low predetermined pressure restarts the pump. A warning unit is described as being operated when the detected battery power is below a predetermined battery power, and warning information relating to pressure is described as being transmitted to an external electronic device. A closely similar electric suction cup has likewise been described, in which the pressure detection unit detects the pressure between the suction cup and the component in real time and the vacuum pump automatically acts again when that pressure is lower than a second predetermined pressure [REF:CN-110630621-B].
10	
11	Hand-carried suction devices that signal something about their own state are also known. A sucker for plate glass has been described having a sucker body defining a suction hole at a suction surface, a manually operatable vacuum pump carried on the body, a sensor communicating with the suction channel that connects the suction hole at the suction surface with the suction hole in the pump, and a sound generator that is turned on through a switch closed by the sensor when the degree of vacuum sensed reaches a predetermined value [REF:US-5184858-A]. The pump in that device is worked by hand rather than electrically, and the sound is generated at a predetermined degree of vacuum which the reference does not relate to the vacuum still needed to retain the sheet.
12	
13	A portable hand grab has been described including one or more suction cups, at least one handle connected to the suction cups for gripping by hand, at least one electrical vacuum pump for at least partially evacuating the suction volume between the suction cups and the attachment surfaces, at least one vacuum sensor for detecting a vacuum level in the suction volume, and an electronic controller configured to control the pump to at least partially evacuate the suction volume when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being less than a preselected minimum vacuum level, optionally together with an attach indicator that the controller activates when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being greater than a preselected safe vacuum level [REF:WO-2017156581-A1]. The signal there tells the user that the vacuum is high enough to attach, and a vacuum below the preselected minimum vacuum level is answered by running the pump again rather than by telling the user that the grip is going.
14	
15	A cordless wand device for grasping objects such as silicon wafers has been described having a housing with a hollow interior, a tip attached to the housing through a hollow tube and having a perimeter region contoured to form an airtight seal against the object, a power source and a vacuum pump positioned within the housing, and light-emitting diodes of different colours which indicate to an operator whether the power source is sufficiently charged to generate sufficient suction force to safely grasp the object, that sufficiency being determined from the voltage drop across resistors connected across the power source [REF:US-5374090-A]. What is indicated in that device is the state of the power source rather than the state of the grip on the object.
16	
17	A portable electric carrying suction cup structure has been described in which a handle is fixed on the upper end of the suction cup body, a vacuum pump is provided on the suction cup body, and a control unit is connected between the power supply part and the vacuum pump, so that air continues to be pumped out after the suction cup body and the material surface have reached an airtight state; the control unit is provided with a pressure gauge by which the user can know the pressure change between the suction cup body and the surface, with a light source for displaying different usage states, and with a buzzer for sending out alarm sounds according to different usage states [REF:CN-2806399-Y]. That reference attributes the avoidance of loosening and falling during movement to the continued pumping, and it describes the buzzer as sounding according to different usage states without relating any sounding condition to the vacuum at which the cup would let go of the material.
18	
19	A digital display suction cup has been described comprising a suction cup and a handle structure, the two ends of the handle structure being provided with a switch button and a pressure relief valve, the handle structure being provided with a battery and a vacuum electric pump which is connected to the suction cup through an air pipe, with an air pressure sensor and a display screen at the lower part of the battery end, a USB charging port electrically connected to the battery, and an inner side of the suction cup provided with an evacuation hole, a pressure relief hole, and a sensing through hole [REF:US-2024424646-A1]. That device monitors and maintains negative pressure in real time and shows the negative pressure value and the battery power on the display screen as numbers for the user to read.
20	
21	Multi-cup handling equipment has been described in which two or more vacuum modules are mounted on a mounting frame, each module having a cup, an electrically powered vacuum pump, a fluid circuit, a controller, and optionally a pressure sensor and a battery, with an interface through which a user selects an operational mode of the modules, and in which each module may include indicators that indicate a functional condition of the module visually or audibly [REF:WO-2022236379-A1].
22	
23	Three shortcomings persist for a person who is holding a panel in one hand. First, the response to a decaying grip in the known powered devices is to run the pump again: the device treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be corrected, and the low pressure value at which it acts is chosen with reference to the working vacuum, not with reference to how much grip is left. If the leak is larger than the pump can make up - a torn lip, a dusty or porous panel, a cracked substrate - the pump simply runs while the grip continues to decay, and the user is told nothing until the panel is gone. Second, where a signal is given, it is given on a condition unrelated to grip (battery state), on a rate of change, on a preset limit whose relationship to the load-holding capacity of the cup is not established, as a confirmation that the vacuum is high enough to attach, or as a number on a display which the user must look at and interpret while carrying a panel. None of these delivers the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.
24	
25	Third, the equipment that has the most elaborate response to a failing grip is the equipment that is not carried in the hand. A suspended plate assembly can be provided with a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that an emergency switch starts [REF:US-5310232-A], and a controller for vacuum lift equipment can limit or alter machine functions in response to sensor feedback [REF:US-10518985-B2]. A lifter that is carried in the hand has none of those remedies available to it: the only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle, and that person can only act if the notice arrives early enough.
26	
27	There remains a need for a cordless, hand-held vacuum lifter that tells the user that the grip is failing while the cup is still holding, so that the warning arrives before the load can be dropped.

Third, the equipment that has the most elaborate response to a failing grip is the equipment that is not carried in the hand. A suspended plate assembly can be provided with a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that an emergency switch starts [REF:US-5310232-A], and a controller for vacuum lift equipment can limit or alter machine functions in response to sensor feedback [REF:US-10518985-B2]. A lifter that is carried in the hand has none of those remedies available to it: the only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle, and that person can only act if the notice arrives early enough.

There remains a need for a cordless, hand-held vacuum lifter that tells the user that the grip is failing while the cup is still holding, so that the warning arrives before the load can be dropped.

**Ledger (traced items).** Authority = `input/disclosure.md` plus the USER turns in `input/conversation.md` (the three "Remove the words QA MARKER ONE" turns and the "begins with the words A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is used to" turn are corrective and add no technical matter); `input/brief.md` for title/inventor/"Not applicable." only.

Traced to exact passages: cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, rigid body 14 with handle 16, suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body, flexible sealing lip 12, electric vacuum pump 20 disposed within the rigid body drawing air through port 22 to create the vacuum, pressure sensor 30 monitoring the grip vacuum, warning indicator 32 driven by the sensor and activating when vacuum is lost and before a load can be dropped, rechargeable battery 40 powering the pump, glass/stone panel 50 ("A cordless handheld vacuum lifter **for glass and stone panels**"), and cordless (no-cord) operation. Claims 1–7 each map to those passages; the method claims recite only the disclosed apparatus performing its disclosed function. Numerals 10/12/14/16/20/22/30/32/40 are used exactly as the inventor assigned them; drafter-added 50, 100, 202–208 are consistent across `numerals.md`, briefs, and description. The previously reported two-level threshold construct, the Summary/Description prior-art passages, and the mis-stated grip-vacuum definition are all gone. No drafting notes, placeholders, or open questions remain. No figure contains a section line, so the section-line designation check is vacuous and passes. FIG. 1's schematic housing/handle loop/broken-off slab and FIG. 3's empty boxes are depiction conventions confined to the briefs.

**Residual defects: four, none critical** — one stale cross-reference to the drawings left behind by the FIG. 4 removal, one spelling inconsistency, one numeral that now covers two acts, and one claimed relationship no figure shows.

input.summary: Full source ledger built from input/disclosure.md and the USER turns of input/conversation.md (brief.md used only for title, inventor, and the two "Not applicable." sections). Every claim limitation, every numbered part, and every structure, relationship, material, position and connection in the description and the three figure briefs traces to an affirmative inventor passage: rigid body 14 with handle 16; suction cup 10 carried by the body; flexible sealing lip 12; electric vacuum pump 20 within the body drawing air through port 22 to create the grip vacuum; pressure sensor 30 monitoring the grip vacuum; warning indicator 32 driven by the sensor, activating on loss of vacuum and before the load can be dropped; rechargeable battery 40 powering the pump; glass or stone panel 50 ("A cordless handheld vacuum lifter for glass and stone panels"); and cordless operation. Claims 1-4 (apparatus) and 5-7 (method of lifting) recite only the disclosed apparatus and its disclosed function. The unsupported two-level warning/release construct, the uncited prior-art passages in the Summary and Detailed Description, and the mis-stated grip-vacuum definition flagged in the earlier round are all absent from the current text. No drafting note, placeholder, open question, or unresolved alternative remains anywhere; the Field section reads naturally and the Background opens with the phrase the inventor required. Numerals 10/12/14/16/20/22/30/32/40 are used exactly as the inventor assigned them, and drafter-added 50, 100 and 202-208 are consistent among numerals.md, the figure briefs, and the description. No figure in this set is a sectional view and no section line is designated anywhere, so the section-line consistency check is vacuous and passes. FIG. 1's schematic housing, looped handle, and broken-off slab, and FIG. 3's four empty boxes, are depiction conventions confined to the briefs; no application text says an outline is shown "by way of example" or that a member may have any closed outline, so nothing of that kind needs removal. Four residual defects remain, none critical and none involving unsupported invention matter. (1) The Detailed Description still asserts that the positive-magnitude grip-vacuum convention "is used consistently in the description, in the drawings, and in the claims", but no drawing in the current set depicts the grip vacuum or any vacuum magnitude - the figure that plotted vacuum levels was removed with the two-level construct, leaving a statement that contradicts the Brief Description. (2) The Background closing sentence writes "hand-held" where every other section, including the title, claims, and abstract, writes "handheld". (3) Numeral 204 is tabulated and briefed as the "evacuating step" but the Detailed Description also folds the separately claimed act of lifting and carrying the panel by the handle into that same numbered step, so 204 does not mean one thing across the numeral table, the FIG. 3 brief, and the description. (4) The relationship "an electric vacuum pump disposed within the rigid body", recited in claims 1 and 5 and in the description, is not shown in any figure: FIG. 1 shows the rigid body 14 but no internal parts, and FIG. 2 shows the pump 20 as a free-standing block with no rigid body in the view. Each is fixed by a self-contained edit that adds no matter beyond the disclosure.

findings.title: Description asserts the grip-vacuum convention is used in the drawings, but no drawing depicts the grip vacuum
findings.where: draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶3 (line 3), final sentence; cf. draft/07-drawings.md lines 1-5 and figures/FIG-1, FIG-2, FIG-3 briefs
findings.detail: The terminology paragraph closes by asserting that the positive-magnitude convention for grip vacuum is carried through the drawings. The current figure set contains no depiction of the grip vacuum or of any vacuum magnitude: FIG. 1 is a side elevation of the lifter against a panel, FIG. 2 is a block diagram of six elements and their connections, and FIG. 3 is four empty step boxes. The figure that plotted vacuum levels was removed together with the unsupported two-level warning/release construct, and this clause was left behind, so the application now states on its face something the Brief Description and the briefs contradict. It is also not curable by adding a vacuum-level drawing, because no inventor passage discloses any vacuum level or magnitude; the nearest source text is only "A pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum" and "activates when vacuum is lost".
findings.evidence: draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶3: "This convention is used consistently in the description, in the drawings, and in the claims." Against draft/07-drawings.md: "FIG. 1 is a side elevation view ... FIG. 2 is a schematic diagram ... showing the suction cup, the port, the electric vacuum pump, the pressure sensor, the warning indicator, and the rechargeable battery. FIG. 3 is a flow diagram of a method of lifting a panel ..." and figures/FIG-2 brief: "each element is a plain rectangle and each connection is a plain line."
findings.fix: In draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶3, replace the final sentence "This convention is used consistently in the description, in the drawings, and in the claims." with "This convention is used consistently in the description and in the claims." Make no change to the figure briefs and add no vacuum-level drawing.

findings.title: "hand-held" in the Background versus "handheld" everywhere else
findings.detail: The closing need statement of the Background hyphenates the term, while the title, Field, Summary, Detailed Description, claims, abstract, numeral table (numeral 100), and all three figure briefs use the unhyphenated form. The same claimed article must carry one spelling throughout the application.
findings.evidence: draft/05-background.md ¶27: "There remains a need for a cordless, hand-held vacuum lifter that tells the user that the grip is failing while the cup is still holding". Compare draft/01-title.md: "Cordless Handheld Vacuum Lifter With Grip-Loss Warning Indicator"; draft/09-claims.md claim 1: "A cordless handheld vacuum lifter, comprising:"; draft/numerals.md: "| 100 | cordless handheld vacuum lifter |".
findings.fix: In draft/05-background.md ¶27, change "a cordless, hand-held vacuum lifter" to "a cordless handheld vacuum lifter". No other change.

findings.title: Numeral 204 is designated the "evacuating step" but the description also assigns the claimed lifting-and-carrying act to it
findings.where: draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶19 (line 19); draft/numerals.md row 204; figures/FIG-3-FLOW-DIAGRAM-OF-THE-METHOD-OF-LIFTING-A-PANEL.md item 2; cf. draft/09-claims.md claim 5
findings.detail: The numeral table and the FIG. 3 brief both define 204 solely as the "evacuating step", and the FIG. 3 box for 204 is one of four boxes standing for four steps. The Detailed Description, however, places two distinct acts inside step 204: drawing air through the port to create the grip vacuum, and lifting and carrying the panel by the handle. Claim 5 recites those as two separate steps ("drawing air through a port ..." and "lifting and carrying the panel by the handle"). The numeral therefore does not carry a single constant meaning across the numeral table, the figure brief, and the description, and the flow diagram silently absorbs a separately claimed step. The fix keeps the lifting and carrying in the description (it is disclosed as the purpose of handle 16 on a handheld lifter for panels) but detaches it from the numbered step, so no figure change is needed.
findings.evidence: draft/numerals.md: "| 204 | evacuating step |". figures/FIG-3 brief: "2. The evacuating step 204." draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶19: "At the evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 and creates the grip vacuum, and the panel 50 is lifted and carried by the handle 16, the panel 50 being retained on the suction cup 10 by the grip vacuum." draft/09-claims.md claim 5: "drawing air through a port with the electric vacuum pump powered by the rechargeable battery, to create a grip vacuum retaining the panel on the suction cup; lifting and carrying the panel by the handle;".
findings.fix: In draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶19, replace the second sentence with two sentences: "At the evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 and creates the grip vacuum. The panel 50 is then lifted and carried by the handle 16, the panel 50 being retained on the suction cup 10 by the grip vacuum." Leave draft/numerals.md and the FIG. 3 brief unchanged.

findings.title: The claimed relationship "electric vacuum pump disposed within the rigid body" is not shown in any figure
findings.detail: Claims 1 and 5 and the Detailed Description recite that the pump is disposed within the rigid body, which is an express inventor statement ("An electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed inside the rigid body 14"). No view illustrates it. FIG. 1 shows the rigid body 14 as a closed outline with no internal part and does not carry numeral 20; FIG. 2 shows the pump 20 as a free-standing rectangle and does not include the rigid body 14 at all. Under 37 CFR 1.83(a) every feature specified in the claims must appear in the drawings. The fix below depicts only what the inventor stated - the pump inside the body - as a plain broken-line rectangle whose position within the schematic housing carries no significance, and adds no other internal structure, no proportion, and no connection.
findings.evidence: draft/09-claims.md claim 1: "an electric vacuum pump disposed within the rigid body". figures/FIG-1 brief: "The rigid body 14 is a closed housing, shown schematically as a generic outlined body in the middle of the drawing area", numerals listed 10, 12, 14, 16, 50, 100 (no 20). figures/FIG-2 brief: "The electric vacuum pump 20 is a rectangle to the right of the port 22", numerals listed 10, 20, 22, 30, 32, 40 (no 14). Inventor passage: "An electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed inside the rigid body 14 and is configured to draw air through a port 22 to create a vacuum."
findings.fix: In figures/FIG-1-SIDE-ELEVATION-OF-THE-LIFTER.md, add a bullet after the rigid-body bullet: "- The electric vacuum pump 20 is inside the rigid body 14 and is therefore drawn in broken lines as a plain rectangle within the outline of the rigid body 14; its position within that outline is not significant and no other internal part is drawn." Add "| 20 | electric vacuum pump |" to that brief's numeral table and "- 20" to its "Numerals shown on this figure" list. In draft/07-drawings.md, amend the FIG. 1 sentence to read: "FIG. 1 is a side elevation view of a cordless handheld vacuum lifter according to an embodiment, shown with the flexible sealing lip seated against a panel and with the electric vacuum pump shown in broken lines within the rigid body." In draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶5, append: "The electric vacuum pump 20, being disposed within the rigid body 14, is shown in broken lines in FIG. 1."
